content: The situation regarding malaria treatment is complex and rapidly evolving, making it difficult to base local treatment guidelines on solid evidence. However, the risks of continuing ineffective treatment regimens likely outweigh the risks of trying new, untested regimens that use generally safe antimalarial drugs, such as artesunate combined with pyronaridine, which may prove effective. Urgent studies are needed to identify the best treatments for artemisinin-resistant malaria. The quality of antimalarial drugs is a critical issue. Poor-quality medicines fall into two categories: falsified drugs, which are counterfeit and often contain little or no active ingredients (sometimes with harmful substances), and substandard drugs, which are produced by legitimate manufacturers but contain incorrect amounts of active ingredients or have degraded due to improper storage or prolonged shelf life. Falsified antimalarial drugs are a significant problem in some regions, as they are often indistinguishable from genuine products at the point of care. These drugs can lead to under-dosing, high treatment failure rates, and the mistaken impression of drug resistance, while also promoting the development of resistance by providing sub-therapeutic blood levels. Some falsified drugs may also contain toxic ingredients. Substandard drugs result from poor manufacturing practices, chemical instability, or improper storage. Artemisinin and its derivatives are particularly prone to chemical instability, which is necessary for their biological action but creates challenges in manufacturing and co-formulation with other compounds. These stability issues are exacerbated under tropical conditions, highlighting the need for stringent quality standards for this class of drugs. Many antimalarial drugs are stored in high heat and humidity and are often sold beyond their expiration dates. In malaria-endemic areas, a large proportion of antimalarial drugs are generic products purchased in the private sector. While these may contain the correct amounts of active ingredients, their formulation may result in inadequate absorption. Antimalarial medicines must be manufactured according to good manufacturing practices, contain the correct drug and excipient contents, demonstrate bioavailability comparable to reference products, be stored under appropriate conditions, and be dispensed before their expiration dates. Tools to assess drug quality at points of sale are being developed, but the capacity of regulatory agencies in many countries to monitor drug quality remains limited. Strengthening legal and regulatory frameworks and fostering collaboration between law enforcement, customs, and regulatory agencies is essential to combat falsified medicines effectively. Private-sector drug distribution outlets should be better informed and actively engaged with regulatory agencies. The World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with other United Nations agencies, has established an international mechanism to prequalify manufacturers of artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) based on their compliance with internationally recommended manufacturing and quality standards. Countries should strengthen their systems for monitoring and evaluating national malaria programs when adapting and implementing these guidelines. These systems should enable countries to track the implementation and impact of new recommendations, better target programs to areas and populations in greatest need, and detect decreasing antimalarial efficacy and drug resistance as early as possible. Routine surveillance is essential, and WHO promotes universal coverage with diagnostic testing, antimalarial treatment, and strengthened malaria surveillance systems. Surveillance and treatment based on confirmed malaria cases will improve understanding of the disease burden and enable national malaria control programs to allocate resources more effectively. Monitoring therapeutic efficacy in falciparum malaria involves assessing clinical and parasitological outcomes of treatment for at least 28 days after starting adequate treatment and monitoring for the reappearance of parasites in the blood. The duration of post-treatment follow-up depends on the elimination half-life of the partner drug in the ACT being evaluated. Molecular genotyping should be used in therapeutic monitoring to distinguish between recrudescence (true treatment failure) and new infections. Antimalarial drug resistance is the ability of a parasite strain to survive and multiply despite the administration and absorption of an antimalarial drug given in recommended doses. Resistance arises due to the selection of parasites with genetic changes that confer reduced susceptibility. Resistance has been documented to all classes of antimalarial medicines, including artemisinin derivatives, posing a major threat to malaria control. Resistance can be prevented or its onset slowed by combining antimalarial drugs with different mechanisms of action and ensuring high cure rates through full adherence to correct dosing regimens. WHO recommends testing the efficacy of firstand second-line antimalarial treatments at least once every 24 months at all sentinel sites. Data collected from these studies inform national treatment policies. National malaria programs should regularly monitor the therapeutic efficacy of antimalarial drugs using standard WHO protocols. The choice of ACTs in a country or region should be based on optimal efficacy, safety, and adherence. Fixed-dose combination formulations are preferred to co-blistered or co-dispensed loose tablets to simplify use, improve adherence, and minimize the availability of oral artemisinin monotherapy. Pediatric formulations should allow accurate dosing without breaking tablets and promote adherence by being acceptable to children. The choice of ACT should also consider local data on therapeutic efficacy, drug resistance, adverse effect profiles, availability of appropriate formulations, and cost. Community case management of malaria is recommended by WHO to improve access to prompt, effective treatment of malaria episodes by trained community members living close to patients. The use of ACTs in this context is feasible, acceptable, and effective. Pre-referral treatment for severe malaria with rectal artesunate and the use of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are also recommended in this context. Health education is vital to optimizing antimalarial treatment. Clear guidelines in local languages, posters, wall charts, educational videos, public awareness campaigns, and information materials for shopkeepers and dispensers can improve understanding of malaria, increase adherence, and reduce unnecessary use of antimalarial medicines. Patient adherence is a major determinant of treatment response, as most treatments are taken at home without medical supervision. Studies suggest that three-day regimens of ACTs are completed reasonably well if patients or caregivers are given adequate explanations at the time of prescribing or dispensing. Pharmacovigilance, the practice of monitoring the effects of medical drugs after they have been licensed for use, is essential to identify and evaluate previously unreported adverse reactions. Governments should have effective pharmacovigilance systems to monitor the safety of all drugs, including antimalarial medicines. Rare but serious adverse drug reactions are often detected only in post-marketing studies or population-based pharmacovigilance systems. More data are urgently needed on the safety of ACTs during the first trimester of pregnancy and on potential interactions between antimalarial and other commonly used medicines. In the final phase of malaria elimination, countries with very low transmission levels require additional interventions to eliminate malaria. Activities in settings approaching elimination will be most effective at reducing transmission if tailored to the distribution of the malaria infection reservoir.
